sec09-R58-card.front: What civil dollar penalty applies to a first ticket under the Red Clay school-bus camera pilot?
sec09-R58-card.expected_back: The handbook’s Red Clay school-bus camera pilot description gives a one hundred dollars civil or administrative assessment for a first violation.

sec09-R59-card.front: What civil assessment applies to each subsequent violation within ten years under the school-bus camera pilot?
sec09-R59-card.expected_back: In that camera-pilot description, each subsequent violation within ten years has a five hundred dollars assessment.

sec09-R60-card.front: How much can be added to a school-bus camera pilot assessment left unpaid for twenty days?
sec09-R60-card.expected_back: The described school district camera pilot may add up to ten dollars when an assessment remains unpaid for twenty days.

sec09-R61-card.front: What is the maximum late-payment fee after forty-five days under the school-bus camera pilot?
sec09-R61-card.expected_back: The camera-pilot late-payment assessment may rise to at most twenty dollars after forty-five days.

sec09-R62-card.front: What maximum late-payment charge applies once a school-bus camera assessment goes unpaid past ninety days?
sec09-R62-card.expected_back: The camera-pilot late-payment assessment may rise to at most thirty dollars after ninety days.

sec09-R63-card.front: Up to how much in court or administrative costs may be added after losing a camera-pilot hearing or missing the deadline?
sec09-R63-card.expected_back: The camera-pilot description permits up to thirty-five dollars in court or similar administrative costs after an unsuccessful hearing or failure to pay or contest on time.

sec09-R64-card.front: Does a civilly assessed school-bus camera pilot ticket count as criminal or affect your driving record and insurance?
sec09-R64-card.expected_back: A civilly assessed violation under the described camera pilot is not criminal and does not enter the driving record or insurance determination.

sec10-F01-card.front: Which four securing steps are required before walking away from a car parked on a street?
sec10-F01-card.expected_back: Before leaving a vehicle parked on a street or highway, shut off its engine, lock the ignition, take the key and apply the brakes.

sec10-F02-card.front: What two additional precautions does the Delaware handbook recommend when leaving a parked car?
sec10-F02-card.expected_back: The handbook also recommends closing the windows and locking the doors when leaving a parked vehicle.

sec10-F03-card.front: How close to the curb or road edge must you park parallel on a two-way highway?
sec10-F03-card.expected_back: On a two-way highway, park parallel to the curb or road edge and no farther than twelve inches away.

sec10-F04-card.front: What should you do before parallel parking if you check your mirror and spot a car following too closely?
sec10-F04-card.expected_back: Before parallel parking, check behind you; if a vehicle follows too closely, continue to another space instead of stopping abruptly.

sec10-F05-card.front: How do you line up your car to begin parallel parking into a curb space?
sec10-F05-card.expected_back: Begin parallel parking by signaling and stopping with your vehicle’s rear aligned with the rear of the vehicle ahead of the desired space.

sec10-F06-card.front: Which way do you steer while reversing first into a right-side parallel-parking space, and where do you aim?
sec10-F06-card.expected_back: For right-curb parallel parking, reverse slowly while steering right to aim your rear toward the vehicle behind the space.

sec10-F07-card.front: Once your front bumper clears the car ahead during right-curb parallel parking, how do you steer?
sec10-F07-card.expected_back: After your front clears the vehicle ahead, steer sharply left and continue reversing slowly until near the vehicle behind.

sec10-F08-card.front: How do you complete a parallel-parking maneuver once your car is inside the space?
sec10-F08-card.expected_back: Finish parallel parking by straightening the wheels, moving forward to center the vehicle, selecting Park, applying the brake and shutting off the engine.

sec10-F09-card.front: Is it legal in Delaware to leave keys inside a running, unattended vehicle?
sec10-F09-card.expected_back: Leaving the keys in a running unattended vehicle is unlawful.

sec10-F10-card.front: How do the steering inputs change when parallel parking along the left curb of a one-way street?
sec10-F10-card.expected_back: For parallel parking at a one-way street’s left curb, reverse the right and left directions in the parking procedure.

sec10-F11-card.front: Which gear should a manual-transmission vehicle be left in when parked facing uphill?
sec10-F11-card.expected_back: Leave a manual-transmission vehicle in low gear when parked facing uphill.

sec10-F12-card.front: Which gear should you select before leaving a manual-transmission vehicle parked facing downhill?
sec10-F12-card.expected_back: Leave a manual-transmission vehicle in reverse when parked facing downhill.

sec10-F13-card.front: What sequence must you follow before pulling out of a parallel-parking space into traffic?
sec10-F13-card.expected_back: Before leaving a parallel-parking space, signal, check traffic, steer toward the open lane and move out gradually.

sec10-F14-card.front: Which two credentials legally authorize parking in a designated accessible space?
sec10-F14-card.expected_back: A designated accessible parking space requires either a displayed rear accessible plate or a parking ID card hanging at the rear-view mirror.

sec10-F15-card.front: What lighting must a vehicle parked along a highway display between sunset and sunrise?
sec10-F15-card.expected_back: A vehicle parked along a highway from sunset to sunrise must display parking lights or, if equipped, four-way flashers.

sec10-F16-card.front: At what daytime visibility threshold must a vehicle parked along a highway turn on parking lights or four-way flashers?
sec10-F16-card.expected_back: Parking lights or equipped four-way flashers are also required along a highway when light is inadequate to see people or objects one thousand feet away.

sec10-F17-card.front: May a parked vehicle leave a single-side turn signal blinking while stationary?
sec10-F17-card.expected_back: A parked vehicle must not flash turn signals on just one side.

sec10-F18-card.front: When is stopping on the paved travel portion of a highway outside business or residential areas allowed, and where must you position the car?
sec10-F18-card.expected_back: Outside a business or residential area, do not park on a highway’s paved or traveled portion unless the vehicle is disabled and immovable; move as far right as possible.

sec10-F19-card.front: Which way must you turn your front wheels when parking facing downhill?
sec10-F19-card.expected_back: For downhill parking, turn the front wheels toward the curb or roadway edge.

sec10-F20-card.front: How must you position your front wheels when parking uphill next to a curb?
sec10-F20-card.expected_back: For uphill parking beside a curb, turn the front wheels away from it and bring the nearer front wheel against the curb.

sec10-F21-card.front: Which way do you turn your front wheels when parking uphill on a road that has no curb?
sec10-F21-card.expected_back: For uphill parking without a curb, turn the front wheels toward the highway edge.

sec10-F22-card.front: How does Delaware law protect passing traffic and bicyclists when exiting a parked car?
sec10-F22-card.expected_back: Do not open a parked vehicle’s door into traffic or danger; use the curb-side door when possible and check for approaching vehicles and cyclists before using the street-side door.

sec10-F23-card.front: What three exceptions excuse stopping in prohibited zones, and does leaving a passenger inside make illegal parking legal?
sec10-F23-card.expected_back: The stopping-and-parking prohibitions allow exceptions for contrary postings, police orders or crash avoidance, and apply even when someone remains in the vehicle.

sec10-F24-card.front: May you stop or park where an official sign prohibits it if no emergency or police order applies?
sec10-F24-card.expected_back: Unless a stated exception applies, do not stop or park where an official sign forbids it.

sec10-F25-card.front: What do a yellow-painted curb or yellow road-edge stripe mean for stopping and parking?
sec10-F25-card.expected_back: Unless a stated exception applies, do not stop or park beside a yellow-painted curb or a yellow road-edge line.

sec10-F26-card.front: How far back from an intersection crosswalk is stopping or parking prohibited?
sec10-F26-card.expected_back: Unless a stated exception applies, stopping or parking is barred within an intersection, directly on its crosswalk, and for twenty feet from that crosswalk.

sec10-F27-card.front: Is stopping or parking two wheels or all four wheels on a sidewalk allowed?
sec10-F27-card.expected_back: Unless a stated exception applies, stopping or parking on a sidewalk is prohibited.

sec10-F28-card.front: May you park or stop across the entrance to a private driveway, alley, or intersecting road?
sec10-F28-card.expected_back: Unless a stated exception applies, do not stop or park in front of a road, alley or driveway, whether public or private.

sec10-F29-card.front: What minimum distance must you leave when stopping or parking near a fire hydrant?
sec10-F29-card.expected_back: Unless a stated exception applies, remain at least fifteen feet from a hydrant when stopping or parking.

sec10-F30-card.front: How close to a fire-station driveway entrance is stopping or parking banned on the same side of the street?
sec10-F30-card.expected_back: Unless a stated exception applies, do not stop or park within twenty feet of a fire-station driveway entrance.

sec10-F31-card.front: When signs are posted across the street from a fire-station entrance, how far does the no-parking zone extend?
sec10-F31-card.expected_back: With signs posted, the stopping-and-parking restriction across from a fire-station entrance extends seventy-five feet, subject to the stated exceptions.

sec10-R01-card.front: How far must you stay from a stop sign, traffic signal, or flashing beacon when stopping or parking?
sec10-R01-card.expected_back: The continued stopping-and-parking prohibition list includes the area within thirty feet of a flashing beacon, stop sign or traffic signal.

sec10-R02-card.front: Where is parking banned around a pedestrian or transit safety island unless signs state otherwise?
sec10-R02-card.expected_back: The continued prohibition list includes the space between a safety island or zone and the curb, plus the area within thirty feet of its end unless posted otherwise.

sec10-R03-card.front: Within what distance of a railroad crossing is stopping or parking prohibited unless posted otherwise?
sec10-R03-card.expected_back: The continued prohibition list includes locations within fifty feet of a rail crossing unless signs state otherwise.

sec10-R04-card.front: When is stopping or parking prohibited beside or across from a street excavation or road obstruction?
sec10-R04-card.expected_back: The continued prohibition list includes parking or stopping beside or opposite a road excavation or obstruction when traffic would be impeded.

sec10-R05-card.front: Is stopping on the street side of another car already parked at the curb ever legal?
sec10-R05-card.expected_back: The continued prohibition list includes the roadway side of a vehicle already stopped or parked at the curb.

sec10-R06-card.front: What parking rule applies on highway bridges, elevated structures, and inside tunnels?
sec10-R06-card.expected_back: The continued prohibition list includes highway bridges, elevated structures and tunnels.

sec10-R07-card.front: What general rule applies to stopping, standing, or parking anywhere that obstructs moving traffic?
sec10-R07-card.expected_back: The continued prohibition list includes any place where stopping, standing or parking obstructs traffic flow.

sec10-R08-card.front: May you park in the median strip or crossover between roadways of a divided highway?
sec10-R08-card.expected_back: The continued prohibition list includes the area between divided-highway roadways, including crossovers.

sec10-R09-card.front: May you stop or park inside a designated fire lane at a store or building?
sec10-R09-card.expected_back: The continued prohibition list includes designated fire lanes.

sec10-R10-card.front: Which two speed standards must every Delaware driver satisfy at the same time?
sec10-R10-card.expected_back: Delaware drivers must satisfy both the general reasonable-speed restriction and specific speed limits.

sec10-R11-card.front: What does Delaware's basic speed rule require when rain, snow, fog, or glare makes the posted limit unsafe?
sec10-R11-card.expected_back: Drive no faster than is reasonable for the actual conditions, even when that requires traveling below the posted limit.

sec10-R12-card.front: Do heavy traffic, bad weather, or running late ever excuse failing to control speed to avoid a collision?
sec10-R12-card.expected_back: Control vehicle speed to avoid striking people, vehicles or other conveyances regardless of weather, traffic density or personal urgency.

sec10-R13-card.front: Can emergency conditions alter statutory speed limits, and may you ever exceed a posted limit?
sec10-R13-card.expected_back: Emergency conditions can change the table’s speed limits, and the posted limit must never be exceeded.

sec10-R14-card.front: What statutory speed limit does the Delaware speed table set for school zones?
sec10-R14-card.expected_back: The handbook’s table lists twenty miles per hour in school zones, with a footnote referring to the code definition of when children are present.

sec10-R15-card.front: What default speed limit applies in Delaware business districts unless posted or altered by emergency?
sec10-R15-card.expected_back: The speed table lists twenty-five miles per hour for business districts, subject to emergency changes and the posted limit.

sec10-R16-card.front: What default speed limit applies in Delaware residential districts unless otherwise posted?
sec10-R16-card.expected_back: The speed table lists twenty-five miles per hour for residential districts, subject to emergency changes and the posted limit.

sec10-R17-card.front: What speed limit does the Delaware table assign to open two-lane roads unless posted otherwise?
sec10-R17-card.expected_back: The speed table lists fifty miles per hour for two-lane roads, subject to emergency changes and the posted limit.

sec10-R18-card.front: What statutory speed limit applies on divided highways and roads with four or more lanes unless posted otherwise?
sec10-R18-card.expected_back: The speed table lists fifty-five miles per hour for divided roads and roads with at least four lanes, subject to emergency changes and posted limits.

sec10-R19-card.front: What default speed limit does the table list for controlled-access expressways and turnpikes unless posted higher or lower?
sec10-R19-card.expected_back: The table lists fifty-five miles per hour for controlled-access highways such as expressways and turnpikes, subject to emergency changes and posted limits.

sec10-R20-card.front: Which two specific Delaware highways are listed at 65 miles per hour in the handbook's speed table?
sec10-R20-card.expected_back: The table lists sixty-five miles per hour for Route one and Interstate four hundred ninety-five, subject to emergency changes and the posted limit.

sec10-R21-card.front: How are drivers notified when authorities reduce an unsafe speed limit for local conditions?
sec10-R21-card.expected_back: Speed limits that are unsafe for prevailing conditions may be reduced, with signs showing the lower limit.

sec10-R22-card.front: When is driving far below normal traffic flow prohibited, and what two reasons excuse slow travel?
sec10-R22-card.expected_back: Do not travel so slowly that normal reasonable traffic is obstructed, unless safety or legal compliance requires that speed.

sec10-R23-card.front: When may you legally travel slower than a posted minimum speed sign?
sec10-R23-card.expected_back: Follow posted minimum speeds unless weather or other conditions make doing so unsafe.

sec10-R24-card.front: What shape and color scheme identify an enforceable legal speed-limit sign?
sec10-R24-card.expected_back: Legal speed-limit signs use black lettering and numerals on white rectangles.

sec10-R25-card.front: What colors are used on advisory-speed signs, and where are they usually mounted?
sec10-R25-card.expected_back: Advisory-speed signs use black lettering on yellow and often appear below warning signs.

sec10-R26-card.front: If an advisory speed plaque is not a statutory limit, what legal consequence can follow if you exceed it and crash?
sec10-R26-card.expected_back: An advisory speed is not a specific limit, but exceeding it and crashing can support a finding that the general speed restriction was violated.

sec10-R27-card.front: Besides cars and trucks, which other users and equipment operators share Delaware highways?
sec10-R27-card.expected_back: Motorists share highways with pedestrians, cyclists, motorcyclists, animal riders or drivers, and farm, road or construction machinery operators.

sec10-R28-card.front: Do traffic laws govern only motor-vehicle drivers, or pedestrians and bicyclists as well?
sec10-R28-card.expected_back: Drivers, pedestrians and bicyclists must all follow traffic laws.

sec10-R29-card.front: When must you stop for a pedestrian at a crosswalk, and when is cautious forward progress permitted?
sec10-R29-card.expected_back: Stop for a pedestrian actively crossing a marked or unmarked crosswalk; cautious progress is permitted when the pedestrian remains safely stopped on the sidewalk as required by law.

sec10-R30-card.front: Does honking your horn satisfy your legal obligation to yield to a pedestrian?
sec10-R30-card.expected_back: Sounding the horn does not replace the duty to yield to pedestrians.

sec10-R31-card.front: How should you respond to pedestrians who are deaf, hard of hearing, or using mobility aids or service animals?
sec10-R31-card.expected_back: Be alert and yield to pedestrians with hearing impairments or physical disabilities using mobility aids or service animals, allowing for additional crossing time.

sec10-R32-card.front: Which two pedestrian areas must you never drive through or block with your vehicle?
sec10-R32-card.expected_back: Do not drive through a pedestrian safety zone or block a crosswalk.

sec11-F01-card.front: What must a driver do for a pedestrian occupying a crosswalk?
sec11-F01-card.expected_back: Yield to a pedestrian in a crosswalk, stopping when required.

sec11-F02-card.front: May you pass a vehicle that has stopped ahead at a crosswalk to let a pedestrian cross?
sec11-F02-card.expected_back: Do not overtake a vehicle that has stopped to let a pedestrian cross.

sec11-F03-card.front: Where should drivers watch with extra care for children, and what speed rule applies near schools?
sec11-F03-card.expected_back: Watch especially carefully for children near schools and homes, and do not speed in school zones.

sec11-F04-card.front: What check is essential right before opening your door and stepping out of a parked vehicle?
sec11-F04-card.expected_back: Check traffic carefully before getting out of a vehicle.

sec11-F05-card.front: Where must a pedestrian walk when a sidewalk is present, and where when no sidewalk exists?
sec11-F05-card.expected_back: Pedestrians must use an available sidewalk; without one, walk on the shoulder facing traffic and as far from the roadway as possible.

sec11-F06-card.front: What visibility item must a pedestrian carry when walking along a Delaware road at night?
sec11-F06-card.expected_back: A pedestrian walking along a road at night must carry a light or reflector.

sec11-F07-card.front: What type of clothing does the handbook recommend for pedestrians whenever practical?
sec11-F07-card.expected_back: Light-colored clothing is recommended for pedestrians when possible.

sec11-F08-card.front: Is walking along a public highway legal while impaired by alcohol or narcotic drugs?
sec11-F08-card.expected_back: Walking on a highway under the influence of alcohol or narcotic drugs is prohibited.

sec11-F09-card.front: May a person stand on a highway to hitchhike or conduct roadside business?
sec11-F09-card.expected_back: Do not stand on a highway to solicit a ride or conduct business.

sec11-F10-card.front: What three-step order of preference should pedestrians follow when choosing where and how to cross a street?
sec11-F10-card.expected_back: Pedestrians should cross at marked crosswalks; when none exists, cross at an intersection; without an intersection, look both ways and cross quickly when needed.

sec11-F11-card.front: What does a blinking DON'T WALK pedestrian signal forbid?
sec11-F11-card.expected_back: Pedestrians must follow WALK and DON’T WALK signals; blinking DON’T WALK prohibits beginning the crossing.

sec11-F12-card.front: Which vehicles must pedestrians watch out for before stepping across an intersection?
sec11-F12-card.expected_back: Before crossing at an intersection, pedestrians must watch for turning cars.

sec11-F13-card.front: When is a pedestrian legally allowed to cross an intersection diagonally from corner to corner?
sec11-F13-card.expected_back: Diagonal intersection crossings are prohibited unless traffic-control signals authorize them.

sec11-F14-card.front: When do pedestrians hold right-of-way at a signalized intersection?
sec11-F14-card.expected_back: Pedestrians have priority at an intersection when their green light or WALK signal permits crossing.

sec11-F15-card.front: Does pedestrian crosswalk priority apply only inside painted lines, or at unmarked crosswalks too?
sec11-F15-card.expected_back: Pedestrians have priority while crossing in either a marked or unmarked crosswalk.

sec11-F16-card.front: Who holds right-of-way where a public sidewalk crosses a driveway, alley, or lot entrance?
sec11-F16-card.expected_back: Pedestrians on a sidewalk have priority as it crosses an alley, driveway or entrance.

sec11-F17-card.front: Which two mobility cues identify a blind pedestrian who holds priority while crossing?
sec11-F17-card.expected_back: Blind pedestrians crossing with a white cane or guide dog have priority.

sec11-F18-card.front: Who must yield when a pedestrian crosses mid-block outside any marked or unmarked intersection crosswalk?
sec11-F18-card.expected_back: Pedestrians must yield when crossing outside a marked crosswalk or an unmarked intersection crosswalk.

sec11-F19-card.front: What right-of-way rule applies if a pedestrian crosses on the asphalt where an overhead bridge or pedestrian tunnel is provided?
sec11-F19-card.expected_back: Pedestrians must yield when crossing a roadway where an overhead crossing or pedestrian tunnel is provided.

sec11-F20-card.front: Which public roadways in Delaware are off-limits to bicyclists?
sec11-F20-card.expected_back: Cyclists may use Delaware public roads except limited-access highways.

sec11-F21-card.front: What does Delaware law allow and require when you pass a bicycle in a lane too narrow to share safely, even with a double yellow center line?
sec11-F21-card.expected_back: When a lane is too narrow for safe side-by-side travel, a motorist passing a bicycle must change lanes, including across a double yellow line, and leave at least three feet.

sec11-F22-card.front: When is a driver allowed to sound the horn at a bicyclist?
sec11-F22-card.expected_back: A motorist must not sound the horn at a cyclist unless danger is imminent.

sec11-F23-card.front: How far to the right should a bicyclist ride under normal conditions?
sec11-F23-card.expected_back: A cyclist should keep right as far as safety permits.

sec11-F24-card.front: What is an intersection bike box, and what two benefits does it give cyclists?
sec11-F24-card.expected_back: A bike box is a designated space at the front of an intersection traffic lane that makes cyclists visible and assists turning.

sec11-F25-card.front: Which turning conflict and crosswalk issue do intersection bike boxes help prevent?
sec11-F25-card.expected_back: A bike box helps prevent conflicts with right-turning vehicles and limits vehicle encroachment on the crosswalk.

sec11-F26-card.front: How does a two-way cycle track arrange bicycle flow along a street?
sec11-F26-card.expected_back: A two-way cycle track separates cycling from motor traffic and carries bicycles both ways along one side of the road.

sec11-F27-card.front: What physical features can separate a curb-height protected cycle track from moving motor traffic?
sec11-F27-card.expected_back: A street-level protected cycle track can use a parking lane or another barrier to separate it from motor traffic.

sec11-F28-card.front: What aerodynamic hazard arises when cars, buses, or trucks pass a cyclist too closely at high speed?
sec11-F28-card.expected_back: Passing too close at higher speeds can create air pressure capable of making a cyclist crash, especially beside a truck or bus.

sec11-F29-card.front: How far over must you move to pass a bike when the lane cannot safely hold your car and the bicycle side by side?
sec11-F29-card.expected_back: If a lane cannot safely fit a vehicle and bicycle together, the passing driver must move fully into another lane, even across double yellow lines.

sec11-F30-card.front: Under what two conditions may you pass a bicycle inside the same unusually wide travel lane?
sec11-F30-card.expected_back: In an unusually wide lane that safely fits both, a driver may pass a bicycle within the lane only while slowing and maintaining at least three feet of clearance.

sec11-F31-card.front: What must you do behind a cyclist on a two-lane road when oncoming traffic or a curve blocks safe passing?
sec11-F31-card.expected_back: On a two-lane road, if sight distance or opposing traffic prevents safe bicycle passing, follow at a safe gap until passing becomes safe.

sec11-F32-card.front: Why must you leave generous room before pulling back right in front of a cyclist you just passed?
sec11-F32-card.expected_back: After passing a cyclist, allow ample clearance before moving back right because the bicycle may be faster than expected.

sec11-F33-card.front: According to Delaware's bicycle-passing rules, what is the sole reason to honk while overtaking a bike?
sec11-F33-card.expected_back: The detailed bicycle-passing rule allows horn use only to warn of an imminent collision.

sec11-F34-card.front: What dangerous maneuver must you never perform right after overtaking a bicyclist?
sec11-F34-card.expected_back: Check carefully for cyclists before entering a road or turning, and do not pass a cyclist only to turn immediately across the bicycle’s path.

sec11-F35-card.front: For which two cycling violations can Delaware hold a parent or guardian legally responsible?
sec11-F35-card.expected_back: Parents or guardians can be responsible for a child’s cycling traffic-law violations and for an under-eighteen child riding without a helmet.

sec11-F36-card.front: Which three handling skills should a bicyclist master before riding alongside street traffic?
sec11-F36-card.expected_back: Before riding in traffic, a cyclist should master straight riding, turns and smooth stops.

sec11-F37-card.front: How should cyclists approach intersections even when traffic rules give the bicycle right-of-way?
sec11-F37-card.expected_back: Cyclists should be prepared to yield to motor vehicles at intersections even when they believe they have priority.

sec11-F38-card.front: Which front and rear devices are mandatory on a bicycle at night, and what extras help?
sec11-F38-card.expected_back: At night, a bicycle requires a white headlamp and red rear reflector; extra reflectors and a red taillamp are helpful.

sec11-F39-card.front: Which three habits define predictable bicycling in traffic?
sec11-F39-card.expected_back: Predictable cycling means traveling with traffic, signaling intentions early and choosing a path that avoids sudden swerves into traffic.

sec11-F40-card.front: Where should a cyclist ride inside an unusually wide lane when comfortable letting cars pass within the lane?
sec11-F40-card.expected_back: In an unusually wide lane, a cyclist should ride on its right side to permit safe in-lane passing when the cyclist feels safe doing so.

sec11-F41-card.front: From what minimum distance must a bicycle's white front headlight be visible at night?
sec11-F41-card.expected_back: A bicycle used at night needs a white headlight visible at five hundred feet.

sec11-F42-card.front: From how far back must a bicycle's red rear reflector be visible at night?
sec11-F42-card.expected_back: A bicycle used at night needs a red rear reflector visible at six hundred feet.

sec11-F43-card.front: Which two options satisfy Delaware's nighttime side-visibility requirement for bicycles, including their distances?
sec11-F43-card.expected_back: Nighttime bicycle side visibility requires either reflective material visible from both sides at six hundred feet or a lamp visible from both sides at five hundred feet.

sec11-F44-card.front: Is a red bicycle taillight legally mandatory or recommended in the Delaware handbook?

sec11-F45-card.front: How must a bicyclist be positioned on the bicycle while riding?
sec11-F45-card.expected_back: A bicycle rider must sit on or astride a permanent seat.

sec11-F46-card.front: When may a bicycle legally carry an extra passenger?
sec11-F46-card.expected_back: A bicycle may carry a passenger only when designed for one.

sec11-F47-card.front: May a bicyclist hold onto or tow behind a moving car or truck on the highway?
sec11-F47-card.expected_back: A cyclist must not cling to another vehicle on the highway.

sec11-F48-card.front: Unlike pedestrians without sidewalks, may a bicyclist ride facing oncoming highway traffic?
sec11-F48-card.expected_back: A cyclist must not ride facing highway traffic.

sec11-F49-card.front: How many hands must a bicyclist keep on the handlebars at minimum while riding?
sec11-F49-card.expected_back: A bicycle rider must keep at least one hand on the handlebars.

sec11-F50-card.front: What two duties apply when a bicyclist approaches pedestrians on a sidewalk or crosswalk?
sec11-F50-card.expected_back: Cyclists must yield to pedestrians on sidewalks and crosswalks and sound an audible warning before passing them.

sec11-F51-card.front: What rule governs wearing headphones or earbuds while riding a bicycle?
sec11-F51-card.expected_back: Cyclists must not use a headset that covers both ears.

sec11-F52-card.front: Under what age must every Delaware bicyclist wear a properly fitted and fastened helmet?
sec11-F52-card.expected_back: Every cyclist younger than eighteen must wear a correctly fitted, fastened bicycle helmet.

sec11-F53-card.front: At how many lanes on an intersecting major road must a bicyclist come to a full stop at a stop sign?
sec11-F53-card.expected_back: A cyclist must stop at a stop sign where the intersecting major road has at least three travel lanes.

sec11-F54-card.front: What must a bicyclist do at a stop sign if a motor vehicle is already stopped ahead at that same sign?
sec11-F54-card.expected_back: A cyclist must stop if a motor vehicle is already stopped at the stop sign the cyclist approaches.

sec11-F55-card.front: What must a cyclist do at a stop sign whenever heavy traffic makes rolling through unsafe?
sec11-F55-card.expected_back: Heavy traffic requiring a stop for safety also requires a cyclist to stop at the sign.

sec11-F56-card.front: How may a cyclist treat a minor-road stop sign when no car is stopped ahead and cross traffic is clear?
sec11-F56-card.expected_back: At a minor-road stop sign without a stopped vehicle ahead, a cyclist may slow, yield to vehicles at or approaching the intersection, and proceed cautiously without stopping.

sec11-F57-card.front: What message does a painted shared-lane bicycle marking communicate to drivers and riders?
sec11-F57-card.expected_back: A shared-lane marking reminds motorists and cyclists that both may lawfully use the lane and supports safe positioning and passing.

sec11-F58-card.front: When is checking blind spots for motorcycles especially critical?
sec11-F58-card.expected_back: Check blind spots frequently for motorcycles, especially before intersection turns or entry from a side road or driveway.

sec11-F59-card.front: How do a motorcyclist's legal rights and duties compare with those of four-wheeled drivers?
sec11-F59-card.expected_back: Motorcyclists have the same roadway rights and responsibilities as other highway users.

sec11-F60-card.front: Why do drivers frequently misjudge an approaching motorcycle?
sec11-F60-card.expected_back: Motorcycles can be difficult to detect, and their distance and speed can be hard for drivers to judge.

sec11-R01-card.front: What should you do before turning left across the path of an oncoming motorcycle?
sec11-R01-card.expected_back: Before turning left across a motorcycle’s path, look again and establish the motorcycle’s position and speed.

sec11-R02-card.front: Why shouldn't you pull out immediately just because an approaching motorcycle's turn signal is blinking?
sec11-R02-card.expected_back: Do not assume a motorcycle’s flashing turn signal guarantees a turn; the rider may have left it on.

sec11-R03-card.front: What minimum following gap does the handbook specify behind a motorcycle below forty miles per hour?
sec11-R03-card.expected_back: When following a motorcycle below forty miles per hour, the handbook specifies a two-second gap.

sec11-R04-card.front: How many seconds of following distance should you keep behind a motorcycle above forty miles per hour?
sec11-R04-card.expected_back: When following a motorcycle above forty miles per hour, the handbook specifies a four-second gap.

sec11-R05-card.front: How should you adjust your following gap behind a motorcycle when pavement is wet or slick?
sec11-R05-card.expected_back: Increase the motorcycle-following gap on a wet or slippery road.

sec11-R06-card.front: May a car share a lane side by side with a motorcycle when extra asphalt seems open?
sec11-R06-card.expected_back: A motorcycle is entitled to a full lane; never drive alongside it within that lane even if there seems to be room.

sec11-R07-card.front: Besides extra following space, what visual hazard should you watch for behind motorcycles during bad weather?
sec11-R07-card.expected_back: Allow extra room behind motorcycles in poor weather and watch for wet-surface glare that can hide the rider.

sec11-R08-card.front: How can strong crosswinds or air blasts from passing tractor-trailers affect a motorcycle?
sec11-R08-card.expected_back: Crosswinds and wind blasts from large trucks can cause sudden changes in a motorcycle’s speed or direction.

sec11-R09-card.front: Why might a motorcyclist suddenly slow down or weave inside the lane on seemingly open pavement?
sec11-R09-card.expected_back: Debris, gravel, pavement seams, animals or manhole covers can cause a motorcycle to change speed or course.

sec11-R10-card.front: What two legitimate moves might a motorcyclist make when crossing rough or angled railroad tracks?
sec11-R10-card.expected_back: A motorcycle rider may slow or alter course to meet angled railway tracks head-on and may rise from the seat over rough tracks.

sec11-R11-card.front: How do metal or open-grate bridge decks affect motorcycle tires and riders?
sec11-R11-card.expected_back: Metal or grated bridges can produce a motorcycle-tire wobble that prompts an inexperienced rider to slow or change direction.

sec11-R12-card.front: Which traffic rights and duties apply to animal riders and drivers of animal-drawn vehicles on Delaware highways?
sec11-R12-card.expected_back: Animal riders and animal-drawn-vehicle drivers share motorists’ highway rights and duties except laws that cannot apply by their nature.

sec11-R13-card.front: How do traffic laws treat operators of farm tractors and self-propelled agricultural equipment on public roads?
sec11-R13-card.expected_back: Drivers of farm tractors and other self-propelled equipment have ordinary motorists’ highway rights and duties, with additional special requirements in a separate supplement.

sec11-R14-card.front: May minibikes, go-carts, golf carts, dirtbikes, motorized scooters, or non-registrable ATVs operate on Delaware highways?
sec11-R14-card.expected_back: Vehicles that the DMV cannot register, such as minibikes, go-carts, golf carts, dirtbikes, motorized scooters and specified all-terrain vehicles, must not be driven on highways.

sec11-R15-card.front: What does a fluorescent orange and red reflective triangle on the back of a vehicle mean, and how should you react?
sec11-R15-card.expected_back: The slow-moving-vehicle emblem is an orange fluorescent and reflective triangle; on seeing it, slow promptly and proceed carefully.

sec11-R16-card.front: What must you verify ahead and behind before pulling out to pass a large truck?
sec11-R16-card.expected_back: Before passing a truck, check ahead and behind and enter the passing lane only where passing is legal and the lane is clear.

sec11-R17-card.front: How can you alert a truck driver before passing, especially after dark?
sec11-R17-card.expected_back: If needed, blink the headlights to alert a truck driver before passing, particularly at night.

sec11-R18-card.front: How quickly should you complete a pass rather than cruising beside another vehicle?
sec11-R18-card.expected_back: Complete a pass promptly instead of remaining alongside the other vehicle.

sec11-R19-card.front: Even if a trucker blinks headlights after you pass, what visual check must you see before pulling back in?
sec11-R19-card.expected_back: After passing a truck, a blink of its headlights can indicate clearance, but return only after seeing the truck’s front in the rear-view mirror.

sec11-R20-card.front: What should you do with your speed immediately after pulling back in front of a truck you passed?
sec11-R20-card.expected_back: Maintain your speed after finishing a pass of a truck.

sec11-R21-card.front: How can you make it safer and faster when a large truck is overtaking your vehicle?
sec11-R21-card.expected_back: When a truck passes, keep to the far side of your lane, consider slowing slightly and do not accelerate.

sec11-R22-card.front: Where should you position your car when meeting a large oncoming truck on an undivided road?
sec11-R22-card.expected_back: When meeting an opposing truck, stay as far to your side as possible to reduce sideswipe risk and turbulence.

sec11-R23-card.front: Does air turbulence between two meeting vehicles pull them together or push them apart?
sec11-R23-card.expected_back: The handbook says turbulence between meeting vehicles pushes them apart rather than drawing them together.

sec11-R24-card.front: What does the term No-Zone describe around a large commercial truck?
sec11-R24-card.expected_back: A truck’s No-Zone refers to danger areas and blind spots around it where collisions are more likely.

sec11-R25-card.front: How should you manage speed and lane return when overtaking any large commercial vehicle?
sec11-R25-card.expected_back: Keep a consistent speed while passing a large vehicle and wait until its cab appears in your rear-view mirror before moving ahead of it.

sec11-R26-card.front: Why must you never slip closely behind a truck that is actively backing up?
sec11-R26-card.expected_back: Never pass closely behind a truck that is backing because both drivers can lose sight of one another in that area.

sec11-R27-card.front: What minimum following time gap should you keep behind a large truck?
sec11-R27-card.expected_back: A truck has a deep blind spot behind it; maintain at least four seconds of following space.

sec11-R28-card.front: Why is cruising alongside either side of a tractor-trailer hazardous?
sec11-R28-card.expected_back: Trucks have large blind spots on both sides, so staying there can leave your vehicle unseen during a sudden lane change.

sec11-R29-card.front: Why might a truck swing left right before an intersection, and what mistake must you avoid?
sec11-R29-card.expected_back: A truck may swing left to turn right; do not cut between it and the curb or right shoulder.

sec11-R30-card.front: What should you do when a truck ahead angles across lanes preparing to back into a loading bay?
sec11-R30-card.expected_back: Do not cross behind a truck preparing to back into a loading area; wait rather than enter the driver’s blind spot.

sec13-F01-card.front: Why must you check your speedometer often right after exiting a fast highway onto a slower local road?
sec13-F01-card.expected_back: Check the speedometer frequently rather than relying on your sense of speed, especially after leaving a high-speed road for a slower local road.

sec13-F02-card.front: What basic duty applies to every posted speed-limit sign along your route?

sec13-F03-card.front: Which two crash risks arise when you slam on the brakes at the last second instead of anticipating stops early?
sec13-F03-card.expected_back: Anticipate stops early because abrupt braking can cause a skid and leaves following drivers less time to avoid a collision.

sec13-F04-card.front: Which two smooth alternatives replace a panic stop when you scan far ahead down the road?
sec13-F04-card.expected_back: Looking far ahead allows gradual slowing or a safe lane change that may avoid a panic stop.

sec13-F05-card.front: How should you brake and steer during an emergency or on slick pavement in a vehicle equipped with anti-lock brakes?
sec13-F05-card.expected_back: For emergency or slippery-road braking with ABS, apply the brakes as firmly as possible and steer if needed to avoid a collision.

sec13-F06-card.front: How must you brake during an emergency or on slippery pavement if your vehicle does not have anti-lock brakes?
sec13-F06-card.expected_back: For emergency or slippery-road braking without ABS, brake as firmly as possible while preventing wheel lock.

sec13-F07-card.front: Which four directional zones around your car require continuous observation for unexpected hazards?
sec13-F07-card.expected_back: Observe the road ahead, both sides and the area behind the vehicle, remaining alert for unexpected events.

sec13-F08-card.front: Besides nighttime darkness, when should you turn on your headlights?
sec13-F08-card.expected_back: Use headlights at night and whenever seeing becomes difficult.

sec13-F09-card.front: Why must you keep interior glances brief, and what must you do before reading a map or route screen?
sec13-F09-card.expected_back: Avoid looking away from the road for more than a few seconds at once; pull safely off the road before consulting a map.

sec13-F10-card.front: What emotional mindset should you keep when another motorist drives aggressively around you?
sec13-F10-card.expected_back: Remain calm and do not take traffic problems personally when dealing with aggressive driving.

sec13-F11-card.front: Which two interpersonal triggers should you avoid around an aggressive driver?
sec13-F11-card.expected_back: Avoid eye contact with aggressive drivers and do not challenge them.

sec13-F12-card.front: What is the safest spacing response when you spot a vehicle weaving, speeding, or behaving erratically?
sec13-F12-card.expected_back: Keep away from drivers behaving erratically.

sec13-F13-card.front: Why does the handbook advise avoiding phone or CB-radio chats while moving, even on hands-free audio?
sec13-F13-card.expected_back: Avoid phone or CB-radio conversations while moving; even hands-free conversation diverts attention from driving.

sec13-F14-card.front: What does Delaware law prohibit regarding headphones or earbuds while operating a motor vehicle?
sec13-F14-card.expected_back: Delaware prohibits driving with headphones or earphones covering or inserted into both ears.

sec13-F15-card.front: How should you drive past a roadside crash, police stop, or work scene instead of slowing just to stare?
sec13-F15-card.expected_back: Do not slow merely to watch a crash, ticket or roadside event; keep watching the road and pass the activity as safely as possible.

sec13-F16-card.front: Which three categories of critical information does active scanning ahead, sideways, and behind reveal early?
sec13-F16-card.expected_back: Scanning ahead, to the sides and behind helps identify approaching hazards, road users and signs.

sec13-F17-card.front: At least how many seconds ahead does the Delaware handbook recommend scanning down the road?
sec13-F17-card.expected_back: Look far enough ahead to prepare for slowing or changing lanes; the handbook recommends looking at least ten seconds ahead.

sec13-F18-card.front: What physical roadway distance does a ten-second look-ahead represent?
sec13-F18-card.expected_back: A ten-second look-ahead means the distance the vehicle will cover during the next ten seconds.

sec13-F19-card.front: How far ahead does a ten-second visual lead roughly correspond to in urban city traffic?
sec13-F19-card.expected_back: In city traffic, the handbook recommends trying to look at least one block ahead.

sec13-F20-card.front: How do you begin checking whether you are actually looking far enough ahead while driving?
sec13-F20-card.expected_back: To measure look-ahead time, choose a stationary roadside object about as far ahead as you are watching.

sec13-F21-card.front: Once you pick a roadside landmark at your gaze horizon, how do you confirm your look-ahead time?
sec13-F21-card.expected_back: Count seconds until reaching that object; the count measures how many seconds ahead you were looking.

sec13-R01-card.front: How does looking well ahead reduce both front-end and rear-end collision risks?
sec13-R01-card.expected_back: Looking well ahead reduces the need for abrupt stops and turns and the risk of striking another vehicle or being struck.

sec13-R02-card.front: How does spotting traffic slowdowns early help your fuel economy?
sec13-R02-card.expected_back: Early observation allows gradual slowing and avoids unnecessary braking that wastes fuel.

sec13-R03-card.front: How does reacting early to traffic ahead benefit drivers following behind you?
sec13-R03-card.expected_back: Acting on traffic changes early gives following drivers more reaction time and helps traffic flow steadily.

sec13-R04-card.front: At which two types of crossings is scanning left and right especially vital?
sec13-R04-card.expected_back: Check to both sides for entering or crossing traffic, particularly at intersections and rail crossings.

sec13-R05-card.front: Beyond street-to-street corners, what everyday access points count as intersections where traffic merges or crosses?
sec13-R05-card.expected_back: An intersection includes places where traffic merges or crosses, such as driveways and parking-area entrances as well as streets.

sec13-R06-card.front: When stopped before an intersection, when should you perform one final left-and-right scan?
sec13-R06-card.expected_back: Before entering an intersection, look left and right for vehicles and pedestrians, checking again immediately before moving from a stop.

sec13-R07-card.front: What space check beyond the crosswalk is required before pulling into any intersection?
sec13-R07-card.expected_back: Check that the path through an intersection is clear enough to avoid stopping and blocking it.

sec13-R08-card.front: Which three checks belong right before turning left across oncoming lanes?
sec13-R08-card.expected_back: Before a left turn across opposing traffic, find a safe gap, check the receiving street for obstacles or pedestrians, and recheck approaching traffic.

sec13-R09-card.front: Which three conflict sources must you check right before making a right turn?
sec13-R09-card.expected_back: Before turning right, check for vehicles from the left, opposing vehicles turning left and pedestrians in the turn path.

sec13-R10-card.front: Why must you still glance left and right when entering an intersection on a green light or priority road?
sec13-R10-card.expected_back: Continue checking both cross-street directions even with a green light or priority sign because other road users may not obey their controls.

sec13-R11-card.front: How should you handle a stop sign where hedges, buildings, or parked vans block your cross-street view?
sec13-R11-card.expected_back: If stopped with a blocked cross-street view, move forward slowly until you can see crossing traffic clearly.

sec13-R12-card.front: Around which six busy roadside environments should you intensify side scanning?
sec13-R12-card.expected_back: Look carefully to the sides near busy sidewalks, shops, parking areas, construction, playgrounds and schools because people or vehicles may enter the road.

sec13-R13-card.front: Why must you slow and look both ways down railroad tracks even on routes where you have never seen a train?
sec13-R13-card.expected_back: At any rail crossing, slow down and look along the tracks both ways; absence of previously seen trains does not mean no train is coming.

sec13-R14-card.front: What far-side clearance condition must exist before your front wheels touch a railroad crossing?
sec13-R14-card.expected_back: Cross tracks only when there is room for the whole vehicle beyond them without blocking the crossing.

sec13-R15-card.front: At a crossing with two or more tracks, why shouldn't you pull out the instant the first train's rear car clears?
sec13-R15-card.expected_back: At a multitrack crossing, wait until the first train is well beyond the crossing because it can conceal another train.

sec13-R16-card.front: During which five driving situations should you check your rear mirrors more frequently than usual?
sec13-R16-card.expected_back: Check rear traffic more often when traffic is heavy and particularly before changing lanes, slowing, reversing or descending a long or steep hill.

sec13-R17-card.front: Which two traffic zones around your car must you check before changing lanes, merging off a ramp, or leaving a curb?
sec13-R17-card.expected_back: Before changing lanes, merging from a ramp or entering from a curb or shoulder, check traffic alongside and behind the vehicle.

sec13-R18-card.front: What do you confirm in your inside and outside mirrors right after signaling an intended lane change?
sec13-R18-card.expected_back: Signal the intended lane change and use rear and side mirrors to confirm the target lane is clear and no one is about to pass.

sec13-R19-card.front: Why must every lane change include a quick head turn over your shoulder in addition to mirror checks?
sec13-R19-card.expected_back: Look over the shoulder toward the planned move to check rear-corner blind spots that mirrors cannot show.

sec13-R20-card.front: How should you manage head checks so looking back does not cause a rear-end crash ahead?
sec13-R20-card.expected_back: Keep lane-change checks brief, rechecking as necessary while continuing to monitor the road ahead and the target lane.

sec13-R21-card.front: In what exact order do you use mirrors and your over-the-shoulder glance when merging or changing lanes?
sec13-R21-card.expected_back: Use mirrors while preparing to merge or change lanes, then check over the shoulder immediately before moving.

sec13-R22-card.front: On a three-or-more-lane highway, why must you also check the lane beyond your target middle lane?
sec13-R22-card.expected_back: Check the lane beyond the target lane because another driver may be moving into the same space.

sec13-R23-card.front: When is glancing at your rear-view mirror while braking especially important?
sec13-R23-card.expected_back: Check behind whenever slowing, especially when braking quickly or slowing somewhere a following driver may not expect.

sec13-R24-card.front: How can parking-lot space selection help you avoid backing hazards altogether?
sec13-R24-card.expected_back: Minimize reversing; a drive-through parking space can let you leave moving forward.

sec13-R25-card.front: What check should you perform before climbing into a parked vehicle that you will have to back out?
sec13-R25-card.expected_back: Before entering a vehicle that must reverse, inspect behind it for children or objects not visible from the driver’s seat.

sec13-R26-card.front: Where should your eyes look while actively backing up your vehicle?
sec13-R26-card.expected_back: When reversing, turn to look directly through the rear window rather than relying only on mirrors.

sec13-R27-card.front: Why should you always keep speed very low while reversing?
sec13-R27-card.expected_back: Reverse slowly because steering is harder while backing.

sec13-R28-card.front: What extra assistance does the handbook recommend using when backing in tight or obscured spots?
sec13-R28-card.expected_back: Use an outside helper for reversing whenever possible.

sec13-R29-card.front: What specific hazard should you watch for in your mirrors while descending a long or steep hill?
sec13-R29-card.expected_back: On long or steep descents, check mirrors and watch for trucks or buses gaining excessive speed.

sec13-R30-card.front: When should you use high-beam headlights at night, and when do traffic conditions require low beams?
sec13-R30-card.expected_back: Use high beams when opposing traffic is absent, while following traffic and heavy traffic call for low beams.

sec13-R31-card.front: Where are high beams particularly helpful at night so long as you dim for approaching traffic?
sec13-R31-card.expected_back: High beams are useful on unfamiliar roads, in construction areas or near roadside pedestrians, subject to the requirement to dim for approaching traffic.

sec13-R32-card.front: By what distance must you dim your high beams for an oncoming vehicle at night?
sec13-R32-card.expected_back: Dim high beams by the time an opposing vehicle is within five hundred feet.

sec13-R33-card.front: Which headlight setting must you use when following behind another car or driving in heavy night traffic?
sec13-R33-card.expected_back: Use low beams while following another vehicle or driving in heavy traffic.

sec13-R34-card.front: Why must you select low-beam headlights rather than high beams in fog, snow, or heavy rain?
sec13-R34-card.expected_back: Use low beams in fog, snow or heavy rain because reflected high-beam light can produce glare.

sec13-R35-card.front: When does Delaware's weather rule require turning your headlights on during daytime or nighttime precipitation?
sec13-R35-card.expected_back: Headlights must be on in rain, mist and snow and whenever the wipers are operating.

sec13-R36-card.front: May you drive using only your amber or dim parking lights instead of full headlights?
sec13-R36-card.expected_back: Do not drive using parking lights alone.

sec13-R37-card.front: What polite cue may you give if an approaching night driver forgets to dim high beams?
sec13-R37-card.expected_back: If an approaching driver uses high beams, briefly flash the headlights a couple of times.

sec13-R38-card.front: Where should you look, and what must you avoid doing, if an oncoming driver refuses to dim high beams?
sec13-R38-card.expected_back: If the other driver does not dim, look toward the right roadway edge and avoid retaliating with high beams.

sec15-F01-card.front: What speed changes should you expect from heavy trucks and underpowered cars on hills or merges?
sec15-F01-card.expected_back: Watch for large trucks and underpowered cars losing speed on steep grades or taking longer to accelerate into traffic.

sec15-F02-card.front: At what speeds do farm tractors, animal-drawn carts, and road-maintenance rigs commonly travel?
sec15-F02-card.expected_back: Farm tractors, animal-drawn vehicles and road-maintenance vehicles commonly travel at twenty-five miles per hour or less.

sec15-F03-card.front: What rear emblem marks slow-moving farm, animal-drawn, or maintenance vehicles?
sec15-F03-card.expected_back: The handbook says these slow vehicles should carry an orange triangular slow-moving-vehicle emblem at the rear.

sec15-F04-card.front: How should you adjust speed in crowded areas with limited room to steer?
sec15-F04-card.expected_back: Reduce speed in crowded places where maneuvering room is limited.

sec15-F05-card.front: Why do shopping centers, parking lots, and downtown streets call for lower speeds?
sec15-F05-card.expected_back: Shopping areas, parking lots and downtown streets can require lower speeds because vehicles and pedestrians move unpredictably in several directions.

sec15-F06-card.front: How should rush-hour congestion and hurried commuters influence your pace?
sec15-F06-card.expected_back: Rush-hour congestion and hurried drivers are reasons to consider slowing.

sec15-F07-card.front: Why can narrow bridges and tunnels require reduced speed?
sec15-F07-card.expected_back: Narrow bridges and tunnels may require slower travel because opposing vehicles pass closer together.

sec15-F08-card.front: What traffic changes must you watch for approaching and leaving toll plazas?
sec15-F08-card.expected_back: At toll plazas, watch for lane changes, stops and acceleration, and for the lane count changing on either side.

sec15-F09-card.front: What hazard must you stay ready for near schools, playgrounds, and residential blocks?
sec15-F09-card.expected_back: Near schools, playgrounds and residential streets, remain ready for children entering the roadway without looking.

sec15-F10-card.front: Which three precautions apply whenever you approach railroad tracks?
sec15-F10-card.expected_back: At railroad crossings, check for trains and space beyond the tracks, slow for rough crossings and avoid blocking the tracks.

sec15-F11-card.front: How does nighttime change object detection and familiar daytime streets?
sec15-F11-card.expected_back: Nighttime reduces how far and how readily a driver can detect objects, and familiar surroundings can appear different.

sec15-F12-card.front: How does oncoming headlight glare affect your eyes after bright beams pass?
sec15-F12-card.expected_back: Approaching-headlight glare can impair vision while the eyes readjust to lower light.

sec15-F13-card.front: What does avoiding outdriving your headlights mean?
sec15-F13-card.expected_back: Avoid outdriving the headlights by choosing a speed that permits stopping within the visible roadway ahead.

sec15-F14-card.front: How should you monitor oncoming vehicles at night without blinding yourself?
sec15-F14-card.expected_back: When meeting vehicles at night, use brief glances to judge their lane position rather than staring into their headlights.

sec15-F15-card.front: What quick visual reference helps keep your lane position steady against night glare?
sec15-F15-card.expected_back: At night, use quick checks to maintain your position and identify the road’s right edge.

sec15-F16-card.front: What must you continue scanning for ahead even while managing oncoming headlight glare?
sec15-F16-card.expected_back: Continue looking ahead for objects in the vehicle’s path while managing nighttime glare.

sec15-F17-card.front: How should you plan around another vehicle displaying a flashing turn signal?
sec15-F17-card.expected_back: Do not assume a flashing turn signal guarantees a turn; plan for the other driver either turning or continuing.

sec15-F18-card.front: Why must you scan cross streets even when cross traffic faces a stop sign or red light?
sec15-F18-card.expected_back: Do not assume every driver will obey a stop sign or red signal.

sec15-F19-card.front: When should you identify shoulders and surrounding escape routes while driving?
sec15-F19-card.expected_back: Continually consider an escape route and note the shoulder and surrounding area before an emergency occurs.

sec15-F20-card.front: How should you react if an oncoming car pulls out to pass without enough room?
sec15-F20-card.expected_back: If an opposing vehicle begins passing without apparent room, slow down and be prepared to use a previously identified escape route if necessary.

sec15-R01-card.front: About how many feet can reacting and stopping from fifty miles per hour take on dry pavement?
sec15-R01-card.expected_back: With good tires and brakes on dry pavement, the handbook estimates that reacting and stopping from fifty miles per hour can require about four hundred feet.

sec15-R02-card.front: About how many feet does the handbook estimate for stopping from thirty miles per hour on dry pavement?
sec15-R02-card.expected_back: Under the stated good-tire, good-brake and dry-pavement conditions, the handbook gives about two hundred feet as a stopping example at thirty miles per hour

sec15-R03-card.front: What danger arises when your sight distance falls shorter than your speed's stopping distance?
sec15-R03-card.expected_back: If sight distance is below the stopping example for a given speed, there may be insufficient time to avoid an object once it becomes visible.

sec15-R04-card.front: What distance limits how fast you may safely drive at night?
sec15-R04-card.expected_back: At night, travel slowly enough to stop within the distance illuminated by the headlights.

sec15-R05-card.front: When heavy rain, snow, or fog cuts sight to two hundred feet or less, what speed ceiling applies?
sec15-R05-card.expected_back: The handbook says visibility limited to about two hundred feet or less in heavy rain, snow or fog does not support speeds above thirty miles per hour

sec15-R06-card.front: What should you do when torrential rain makes seeing the road safely impossible?
sec15-R06-card.expected_back: If rain becomes too heavy to see well enough to drive, pull off in a safe place and wait for it to clear.

sec15-R07-card.front: Why must you ease off speed approaching a view-blocking hill crest or curve?
sec15-R07-card.expected_back: Slow for a hill or curve that hides the roadway so a stop remains possible for an unseen obstruction.

sec15-R08-card.front: Why should you steer with maximum safe clearance past a line of parked vehicles?
sec15-R08-card.expected_back: Give parked vehicles as much safe clearance as possible because they obscure people exiting or walking between them.

sec15-R09-card.front: What does Delaware's four-second sight-distance rule test?
sec15-R09-card.expected_back: The four-second sight-distance rule checks whether vehicle speed is too high for how far ahead the driver can see.

sec15-R10-card.front: How do you perform the four-second sight-distance check on the road?
sec15-R10-card.expected_back: Choose a stationary object at the farthest clearly visible point and count four seconds while approaching it.

sec15-R11-card.front: What must you do if your car reaches your sight-distance landmark before four seconds finish?
sec15-R11-card.expected_back: If you reach the sight-distance marker before four seconds have elapsed, slow down because speed is too high for the visible distance.

sec15-R12-card.front: How does the four-second sight-distance check help specifically after dark?
sec15-R12-card.expected_back: Use the four-second sight-distance check at night to avoid outdriving the headlights.

sec15-R13-card.front: Which roadway realities are built into posted speed limits?
sec15-R13-card.expected_back: Obey speed limits because they reflect road design, vehicle use and hidden entry points as well as traffic volume.

sec15-R14-card.front: What weather and traffic conditions do posted speed-limit signs assume?
sec15-R14-card.expected_back: Posted limits assume ideal conditions; wet or icy pavement, poor vision or heavy traffic can require a lower speed.

sec15-R15-card.front: Can you receive a speeding citation while driving below the posted speed limit?
sec15-R15-card.expected_back: A driver can be ticketed for speed that is unsafe for conditions even while below the posted limit.

sec15-R16-card.front: What benefit does keeping open space around your vehicle create?
sec15-R16-card.expected_back: Maintaining space around the vehicle creates a time cushion for reacting to other road users.

sec15-R17-card.front: How does Delaware distinguish the three-second rule from the four-second check?
sec15-R17-card.expected_back: The three-second rule is introduced as a way to judge following distance, distinct from the four-second sight-distance check.

sec16-F01-card.front: How do you time your following distance behind a leading vehicle?
sec16-F01-card.expected_back: Measure following time from when the leading vehicle’s rear passes a fixed roadside point until your vehicle reaches that point.

sec16-F02-card.front: What must you do if your car reaches the roadside marker before three seconds finish?
sec16-F02-card.expected_back: If your vehicle reaches the marker before three seconds pass, fall back and repeat the check until the gap reaches at least three seconds.

sec16-F03-card.front: How many seconds of following distance may demanding conditions require beyond the baseline?
sec16-F03-card.expected_back: Some conditions can require more than the baseline following space; the handbook says a four-second gap may be needed.

sec16-F04-card.front: Why must you widen your following gap on slippery roads?
sec16-F04-card.expected_back: Increase following space on slippery roads because stopping takes more distance.

sec16-F05-card.front: How should you respond when a trailing driver pulls out to overtake your vehicle?
sec16-F05-card.expected_back: If a following driver wants to pass, slow to create room ahead and help the pass finish sooner.

sec16-F06-card.front: Why should you leave extra space behind a motorcycle, especially on wet, icy, gravel, or metal surfaces?
sec16-F06-card.expected_back: Leave extra room behind motorcycles in case the rider falls, particularly on wet, icy, gravel or metal surfaces.

sec16-F07-card.front: Behind which tall or towing vehicles should you drop farther back because drivers may miss you?
sec16-F07-card.expected_back: Fall farther behind vehicles whose drivers may not see you, including trucks, buses, vans and vehicles towing campers or trailers.

sec16-F08-card.front: What two visibility advantages come from holding a wider gap behind a large vehicle?
sec16-F08-card.expected_back: A larger gap behind a large vehicle improves the view ahead and the chance of being seen.

sec16-F09-card.front: How does carrying a heavy load or pulling a trailer affect your own following distance?
sec16-F09-card.expected_back: A heavy load or towed trailer increases stopping distance and calls for more following space.

sec16-F10-card.front: How should you adjust following distance when darkness or foul weather obscures the road ahead?
sec16-F10-card.expected_back: Increase following distance when darkness or bad weather makes the road ahead hard to see.

sec16-F11-card.front: How should you adjust your front gap when another driver tailgates closely behind you?
sec16-F11-card.expected_back: When tailgated, try to create additional space ahead so braking can be less abrupt.

sec16-F12-card.front: Why must you hold extra following room behind police cars, ambulances, and fire trucks?
sec16-F12-card.expected_back: Leave extra room behind police, ambulance and fire vehicles because they need operating space.

sec16-F13-card.front: Behind which three vehicle types must you leave extra room approaching railroad crossings?
sec16-F13-card.expected_back: Near rail crossings, leave additional room behind vehicles that must stop there, including transit buses, school buses and hazardous-material carriers.

sec16-F14-card.front: Why should you leave extra bumper room when stopped behind another car on an uphill slope?
sec16-F14-card.expected_back: When stopped uphill, leave room for the vehicle ahead to roll backward as it starts.

sec16-F15-card.front: Which two driving habits help trailing motorists maintain a safe gap behind you?
sec16-F15-card.expected_back: Maintain a steady speed and signal slowing or turns early to help following drivers keep a safe gap.

sec16-F16-card.front: Where should you stop to pick up or let out passengers?
sec16-F16-card.expected_back: Pick up or release passengers at a safe stopping place outside traffic.

sec16-F17-card.front: How should you handle trailing traffic before backing into a parallel parking space?
sec16-F17-card.expected_back: Before parallel parking with traffic behind, signal, draw beside the space and allow following vehicles to pass.

sec16-F18-card.front: What should you do when necessary slow driving delays traffic behind you?
sec16-F18-card.expected_back: If necessary slow travel delays others, pull aside safely and let them pass, using a turnout where available.

sec16-F19-card.front: How can you encourage a tailgater to pass on a multilane road versus a single-lane road?
sec16-F19-card.expected_back: If tailgated and a right lane is available, move right; without one, wait for a clear road ahead and gradually reduce speed.

sec16-F20-card.front: Why must you never slam your brakes to warn off a tailgater?
sec16-F20-card.expected_back: Never brake abruptly to discourage a tailgater because this increases rear-impact risk.

sec16-F21-card.front: Why shouldn't you cruise right alongside another vehicle on a multilane road?
sec16-F21-card.expected_back: Maintain side space and avoid remaining alongside another vehicle where it could crowd or enter your lane.

sec16-F22-card.front: Where in your lane should you avoid riding on a two-lane road with opposing traffic?
sec16-F22-card.expected_back: Leave as much safe room as possible from opposing vehicles; on a two-lane road, avoid hugging the center line.

sec16-F23-card.front: Where inside your travel lane does the Delaware handbook generally advise driving?
sec16-F23-card.expected_back: The handbook generally recommends driving in the center of the lane.

sec16-F24-card.front: How can you help ramp traffic merge onto a multilane highway when the next lane over is clear?
sec16-F24-card.expected_back: On a multilane road, make room for entering traffic by moving over when the neighboring lane is clear.

sec16-F25-card.front: Which three sudden hazards justify leaving extra room beside parked cars?
sec16-F25-card.expected_back: Leave extra clearance beside parked cars because doors, pedestrians or the vehicles themselves may enter your path.

sec16-F26-card.front: Why do pedestrians and bicyclists, especially children, require extra lateral space?
sec16-F26-card.expected_back: Allow extra room for pedestrians and cyclists, especially children, because they can enter the path suddenly.

sec16-R01-card.front: How should you position your car between two non-vulnerable hazards on opposite sides?
sec16-R01-card.expected_back: When vulnerable users are not involved, the handbook advises a middle course between two hazards, with additional clearance toward the more dangerous side.

sec16-R02-card.front: How should you handle an oncoming car arriving right as you reach a cyclist ahead?
sec16-R02-card.expected_back: Address hazards separately when possible; if an opposing vehicle approaches while you intend to pass a bicycle, slow and let it pass first.

sec16-R03-card.front: At least how many feet of clearance must you keep when passing a cyclist, and what should you use on multilane roads?
sec16-R03-card.expected_back: When passing a cyclist, preserve at least three feet of clearance and use the neighboring lane on a multilane road whenever possible.

sec16-R04-card.front: Why must you reject squeezing into a tight merge gap?
sec16-R04-card.expected_back: Do not merge into an undersized gap; choose enough room to maintain a safe space cushion.

sec16-R05-card.front: How must you cross several lanes on a wide roadway?
sec16-R05-card.expected_back: When crossing several lanes, change one lane at a time rather than trying to cross them all at once.

sec16-R06-card.front: How do gap requirements differ between crossing straight across a road and turning into its flow?
sec16-R06-card.expected_back: A crossing maneuver needs room to clear the whole road, while entry needs room to turn and accelerate.

sec16-R07-card.front: When is stopping halfway across a divided highway median acceptable?
sec16-R07-card.expected_back: Stop partway across only in a median large enough to contain the entire vehicle without protruding into traffic.

sec16-R08-card.front: Beyond oncoming gaps, what must you check along your target street before starting a left turn?
sec16-R08-card.expected_back: Before turning left across opposing traffic, ensure the intended path is not blocked by vehicles or pedestrians.

sec16-R09-card.front: May you pull into a backed-up intersection on a green light, and what penalty can follow?
sec16-R09-card.expected_back: Do not enter a blocked intersection even on green; blocking it can result in a ticket.

sec16-R10-card.front: When another vehicle flashes a turn signal near your corner, when is it safe to pull out?
sec16-R10-card.expected_back: Do not assume another driver will create a gap or turn because a signal is flashing; wait for the turn to begin and proceed only when safe.

sec16-R11-card.front: Why might a motorcycle's turn signal keep flashing even when the rider plans to go straight?
sec16-R11-card.expected_back: A motorcycle’s signal may remain on from an earlier turn because it may not cancel automatically.

sec16-R12-card.front: What clearance condition must be met before you drive onto railroad tracks?
sec16-R12-card.expected_back: Cross rail tracks only when you can clear them without stopping on the tracks.

sec16-R13-card.front: Where is overtaking allowed, and how many vehicles does the handbook generally advise passing at once?
sec16-R13-card.expected_back: Pass only where signs and markings permit and there is enough space; the handbook generally recommends passing one vehicle at a time.

sec16-R14-card.front: Roughly how many seconds of clear opposing road does a fifty-five-mile-per-hour pass require?
sec16-R14-card.expected_back: The handbook’s passing example at fifty-five miles per hour calls for roughly ten seconds of clear opposing traffic and sight distance, with the driver still judging whether space is adequate.

sec16-R15-card.front: How far does one vehicle travel during ten seconds at fifty-five miles per hour?
sec16-R15-card.expected_back: At fifty-five miles per hour, a vehicle covers more than eight hundred feet in ten seconds.

sec16-R16-card.front: How much road do you and an oncoming fifty-five-mile-per-hour car close together in ten seconds, and what if unsure?
sec16-R16-card.expected_back: When both vehicles in the example travel at fifty-five miles per hour, together they cover over one thousand six hundred feet during ten seconds; uncertainty about adequate passing space calls for waiting.

sec16-R17-card.front: Within what distance of a blind hill or curve does the handbook advise against starting a pass?
sec16-R17-card.expected_back: The handbook advises against beginning a pass within one-third mile of a view-blocking hill or curve because opposing traffic may be hidden.

sec16-R18-card.front: Why is passing hazardous near intersections, railroad crossings, or shopping-center entrances?
sec16-R18-card.expected_back: Passing near intersections, rail crossings or shopping-area entrances is dangerous because other road users can enter unseen or not expect opposing-lane traffic.

sec16-R19-card.front: What roadside or traffic factors should you scan ahead for before pulling out to pass?
sec16-R19-card.expected_back: Before passing, look for roadway restrictions or traffic that could push another vehicle into the passing space.

sec16-R20-card.front: Which roadside obstacles can shrink available passing room ahead?
sec16-R20-card.expected_back: People or bicycles near the road, a narrowed bridge, ice, potholes or other obstructions can reduce available passing space.

sec16-R21-card.front: What lane-return requirement must be met before you start overtaking?
sec16-R21-card.expected_back: Do not pass unless there is room to return to the proper lane without relying on other drivers to make space.

sec16-R22-card.front: May you overtake another vehicle when approaching a railroad crossing?
sec16-R22-card.expected_back: Do not pass with a railroad crossing ahead.

sec16-R23-card.front: What interior mirror check tells you there is enough room to pull back in after passing?
sec16-R23-card.expected_back: Before returning after a pass, leave adequate clearance; the handbook uses seeing both passed-vehicle headlights in the rear-view mirror as a clearance cue.

sec16-R24-card.front: How should you drive past intersections or driveways where cross-drivers have blocked views?
sec16-R24-card.expected_back: Allow extra room for drivers with obstructed views at intersections or driveways.

sec16-R25-card.front: Why do reversing vehicles and cars entering or exiting parking stalls need extra space?
sec16-R25-card.expected_back: Give extra room to drivers reversing into the road or entering and leaving parking spaces because they may not see you.

sec16-R26-card.front: Which visual clues warn you a driver or pedestrian cannot see surrounding traffic clearly?
sec16-R26-card.expected_back: Drivers with obscured windows and pedestrians with faces hidden by hats or umbrellas may need extra space.

sec16-R27-card.front: Around which busy or distracted groups should you widen clearance and caution?
sec16-R27-card.expected_back: Allow additional room or caution around distracted people, including delivery workers, construction workers, inattentive children and drivers.

sec16-R28-card.front: Which behaviors mark a confused driver who needs extra space?
sec16-R28-card.expected_back: Give extra room to potentially confused drivers, such as those searching for addresses, slowing inexplicably or appearing unsure of direction.

sec16-R29-card.front: What should you do if another motorist misjudges a pass and runs short of room?
sec16-R29-card.expected_back: If another driver attempts a pass without enough room, slow and allow a safe return rather than making the mistake worse.

sec16-R30-card.front: How should you respond when a nearby driver urgently needs to merge into your lane?
sec16-R30-card.expected_back: If a driver suddenly needs to change lanes, slow to allow the merge when needed to avoid a collision.

sec17-F01-card.front: Which five personal factors determine whether you are fit to drive?
sec17-F01-card.expected_back: Driving fitness depends on clear vision, adequate rest, freedom from alcohol or drug impairment, general health and emotional readiness.

sec17-F02-card.front: How does poor vision affect hazard handling in traffic?
sec17-F02-card.expected_back: Poor vision can make traffic, road conditions and developing hazards harder to identify and respond to promptly.

sec17-F03-card.front: What minimum visual acuity passes Delaware's licensing vision screening?
sec17-F03-card.expected_back: The handbook lists at least twenty over forty vision in one eye, with or without corrective lenses, as the vision-screening passing criterion.

sec17-F04-card.front: What driving restriction applies to Delaware applicants with twenty-over-fifty vision?
sec17-F04-card.expected_back: The handbook states that drivers with twenty over fifty vision are limited to daylight driving.

sec17-F05-card.front: What helps peripheral vision catch side hazards while you look ahead?
sec17-F05-card.expected_back: Peripheral vision helps detect hazards at the sides while looking ahead, but side mirrors and occasional side glances are also needed.
